Reproducing gQLS on 30 Hurricanes — and what it does to the 1-in-100

On the 30 most-damaging US hurricanes (Pielke-Landsea 1998, normalized 1995 USD), does a from-scratch gQLS reproduce Adjieteh (2024) Table 6.9 within the published reporting resolution; does its robustness advantage over MLE survive the thesis's 10x contamination and leave-top-k-out stress; and does that advantage carry into per-event return levels - the thesis's own declared future work?

study: 06-hurricane-gqls-returnlevels · metric: mean_abs_param_deviation (reproduction), return_level_instability_pct (decision) · domain: insurance · 2026-07-31

1. The Question 2. The Method 3. The Data 4. The Journey 5. Findings 6. Coding Advice 7. Next Steps

The Question

A catastrophe pricing actuary has thirty numbers: the thirty most damaging hurricanes to hit the United States between 1900 and 1995, each normalized to 1995 dollars for inflation, wealth and coastal population. From those thirty numbers a committee wants one number — the 1-in-100 event loss — and that number will set a catastrophe layer, a capital charge, or a solvency return.

Now suppose one of the thirty rows is wrong. Not missing, not obviously absurd — just wrong by a factor of ten, the way a decimal-point slip or a double-counted recovery makes a number wrong. No data-quality process catches it, because $723bn for the 1926 Great Miami hurricane is only implausible if you already know the answer.

How much does the 1-in-100 move? And is there an estimator that would not have moved at all?

A 2024 doctoral thesis says yes and shows the parameters standing still. It never carries those parameters through to a return level. That gap — between a robust parameter and a stable decision — is what this study exists to measure. The registered goal:

On the 30 most-damaging US hurricanes (Pielke-Landsea 1998, normalized 1995 USD), does a from-scratch gQLS reproduce Adjieteh (2024) Table 6.9 within the published reporting resolution; does its robustness advantage over MLE survive the thesis's 10× contamination and leave-top-k-out stress; and does that advantage carry into per-event return levels — the thesis's own declared future work?

Two tracks, because there are two different objects here

The goal contains two questions that a single leaderboard would silently blend. Klein answers that with tracks: independent metric frontiers that are never merged, each owning its own direction, its own measured minimum_delta, and its own guardrails.

TrackMetricWhat it measuresminimum_deltaGuardrails
reproduction mean_abs_param_deviation (lower) Distance-to-published. Mean |Δθ| over the 36 published Table-6.9 parameters — a property of our implementation, not of the data. 0.005 — half the last published digit max |Δθ| ≤ 0.02 · max |ΔW| ≤ 0.10 · max |Δp| ≤ 0.02 · wall_seconds ≤ 120
decision return_level_instability_pct (lower) Decision stability. Max |% change| of the fitted 1-in-100 event loss across the adaptive stress set — the actuarial decision unit. 1.0 pp — an ordering device, see below w_pvalue ≥ 0.10 · wall_seconds ≤ 120

Two design choices in that table are load-bearing and worth stating explicitly.

Why the reproduction metric is not a goodness-of-fit statistic. The obvious metric for "did we implement this right" is something like a W statistic or an AIC. It would be the wrong object. A GoF statistic measures whether the model fits the data; this track asks whether our code reproduces their printed table. Those are different questions with different failure modes, and only the second one can be answered against 156 numbers that were fixed in print before this study existed. The mean over 36 parameters keeps the frontier well-behaved as specification bugs get fixed; the max guardrail exists so that one broken cell cannot hide behind a good average. Section 4 shows the max guardrail earning its keep twice — once on a real bug, once on something that turned out not to be ours at all.

The w_pvalue guardrail is an anti-degeneracy device. On a stability metric, the trivially optimal model is one that predicts nothing: an estimator whose 1-in-100 never moves because it never responds to anything would score 0.0 and win. Requiring the in-sample goodness-of-fit test to PASS (W p ≥ 0.10) turns the question into the one an actuary actually asks: among models that FIT, which gives the most stable 1-in-100? Without it, the decision track would have been a race to the most useless model.

Six research questions, each with a prior registered before the loop

Every prior below was written into study.yaml before any experiment ran, so every one of them could come out wrong. Three did — including the one the study was built to ask.

RQQuestionRegistered prior
RQ1Does a from-scratch gQLS reproduce all 36 parameters of Table 6.9 within the 0.005 reporting resolution?Yes — the specification is complete once eq. 3.8 and the standard-member table are used (pre-verified at the method gate)
RQ2Is the thesis's B=1000 parametric bootstrap for W_out necessary, or are its published p-values indistinguishable from a χ²r−2 reference?Indistinguishable to ≤ 0.02 — five families cross-checked during planning
RQ3Does the thesis's 10× contamination move gQLS parameters by less than the reporting resolution while MLE-lognormal σ̂ moves 0.83 → 1.10?Yes for gQLS — breakdown point min{a, 1−b} = 0.05 > 1/30
RQ4Under leave-top-k-out (k = 1,2,3) — a stress the thesis never runs — does gQLS stability degrade exactly where the breakdown point predicts?k ≤ 1 stable at (0.05, 0.95); k = 2 breaches that trim but not (0.10, 0.90)
RQ5Among configurations that PASS the in-sample GoF test, which estimator × family gives the most stable 1-in-100 event loss?Genuinely uncertain. log-Cauchy fits best but its quantile transform amplifies σ̂ by tan(0.49π) = 31.8 at p = 0.99. The best-fitting model may be the least decision-stable — the study's sharpest open question
RQ6Does robustness at the parameter level transfer to robustness at the decision (return-level) level?Partially — the quantile transform can undo parameter robustness for heavy-tailed families (uninformed)

RQ1–RQ3 are reproduction: they ask whether the published work can be rebuilt from its own description. RQ4–RQ6 are extension: no published work carries these fits through to a 1-in-100 event loss, and none runs a leave-top-k-out stress on this sample. The thesis's own §7.2 names risk measures as future work, so the second half of the study is genuinely new rather than a re-derivation.

The sealed design — and the honesty it demands

Klein seals a final-test partition and allows each track exactly one access to it. With n = 30 there is no partition to hold out; you cannot spare six hurricanes. So this study seals something else: published third-party numbers. Adaptive work was contractually confined to Table 6.9 (36 parameters). The sealed reproduction target was the full Table 6.10 grid — 5 estimator arms × 6 families × original and 10×-modified data = 60 cells, 120 parameters the loop never touched. The sealed decision target was the thesis's exact modification (72.303 → 723.03); adaptive stress was capped at 5×.

That is a genuinely strong anti-peeking guarantee in one direction. The targets are third-party numbers fixed in print before the study existed: they cannot be moved by anything the study does, and unlike a random fold, an analyst cannot in principle inspect them ahead of time without breaking the contract. But the design is structurally blind in another direction, and the data card wrote the constraint before any modeling began. It is carried here verbatim because it is exactly the sentence that erodes first in a slide deck:

Standing rule (e). “Sealed evidence = independent PUBLISHED TARGETS, not independent data — confirmation wording is ‘implementation fidelity + within-sample robustness’, never out-of-sample generalization.” The same 30 observations underlie both the adaptive and the sealed evaluation, so sampling error is fully common-mode and the sealed test is structurally blind to it.

Read every confirmed label in section 5 through that rule. It means our implementation reproduces their published numbers on their sample, and the estimator is robust within that sample. It never means the next hurricane sample will behave the same way.

One further consequence, registered up front rather than discovered later: the decision track's minimum_delta of 1.0 pp is an ordering device on a fixed 30-event sample, not a confidence statement. At n = 30 a parametric bootstrap puts σ̂ = 0.8339 inside [0.617, 1.034] — a ±25% relative band on the single parameter that drives the entire tail. Every instability percentage in this report ranks estimators on these thirty events under this stress. Section 2 explains why that delta was kept at 1.0 rather than quietly shrunk to manufacture significance.

The Method

The whole method fits in one sentence, and the sentence is worth memorizing before any of the algebra:

gQLS is a Q-Q plot fitted by generalized least squares.

You already do the first half by hand. Take your losses, plot the empirical quantiles against the theoretical quantiles of a candidate law, and eyeball whether the points fall on a line. If they do, the intercept of that line is your location parameter and the slope is your scale parameter. Quantile least squares (QLS) stops eyeballing and runs the regression. The g — generalized — runs it with the right error covariance instead of pretending the plotted points are equally reliable and mutually independent.

Why a small set of quantiles buys robustness

Point maximum likelihood at the 30 hurricane losses and every observation gets a vote, weighted by the score function — including the 1926 Great Miami storm at $72.303bn, which is 2.185× the second-largest loss in the sample and 20.5% of the total damage mass on its own. The MLE has no mechanism for saying “that one is unusual.” Inflate that single number tenfold and the lognormal σ̂ moves from 0.833868 to 1.097494 — a +31.6% shift in the one parameter that governs the entire tail, from one corrupted record out of thirty.

QLS never looks at that observation. It reads the sample at k = 8 probability levels between a = 0.05 and b = 0.95 and fits the quantile curve through those eight points. The largest observation sits above p = 0.95; nothing in the estimating equations consults it. Corrupt it, delete it, multiply it by a million — the estimate does not move. That is not a heuristic. It is the definition of a breakdown point:

BP = min{a, 1 − b} — the fraction of the sample you may corrupt arbitrarily before the estimate can be driven anywhere.

Read it as a count, because that is what makes it actionable. At (a, b) = (0.05, 0.95) the breakdown point is 5%, and 5% of 30 events is 1.5 — so one corrupted event is tolerated and two are not. At (0.10, 0.90) it is 10%, so three are tolerated. The trim you choose is the number of bad records you are buying protection against. There is no free lunch: the same trim that ignores the corrupted maximum also ignores the genuine maximum.

The figure below makes the trim visible. Hollow marks are all 30 order statistics at their display positions; filled marks are the eight estimation-grid levels the gQLS fit actually consults. Everything outside the filled marks is what the trim protects you from — and, symmetrically, what it declines to learn from.

Why the “generalized” matters

Ordinary QLS (oQLS) runs plain OLS on that Q-Q plot. That silently assumes the eight plotted points are equally reliable and mutually independent. They are neither. Sample quantiles in the sparse tail wobble far more than sample quantiles near the median, and adjacent quantiles from the same sample are strongly positively correlated — they share order statistics.

The fix is generalized least squares: down-weight the noisy points and account for the correlation. GLS normally stalls right here, because you would have to estimate the error covariance from the data — and estimating a k×k covariance from 30 points is worse than the disease. In this problem you do not have to. Serfling's joint asymptotic normality theorem hands you the covariance of the empirical quantile vector in closed form, and after standardization it depends only on the standard member of the family — no unknown parameters at all. You can write Σ★ down before seeing a single data point.

How much does that buy? The thesis's asymptotic relative efficiencies (k = 25, (0.05, 0.95)) answer bluntly:

Standard memberoQLS AREgQLS ARE
Normal0.9360.911
Gumbel0.9020.893
Logistic0.7040.955
Laplace0.7570.947
Cauchy0.2320.995

For a heavy standard member, ordinary QLS throws away roughly 77% of the available information and gQLS throws away almost none. That is the single largest effect in this method. And it is directly visible in the data being reproduced: on the hurricane sample at (0.05, 0.95), log-Cauchy's σ̂ is 0.229912 under oQLS and 0.485055 under gQLS — a factor of 2.11 from the weighting alone. That split is this study's specification falsifier: if a from-scratch Σ★ is wrong, those two numbers will not separate that way. Section 4 shows it passing at a deviation of 8.8e−05.

Read the Normal row too, because it is the honest counterweight: gQLS is very slightly worse than oQLS there. For a light, well-behaved member the identity-matrix pretence costs almost nothing, and the GLS weighting's finite-sample overhead is not repaid. The gain is concentrated exactly where the tail is heavy — which is where loss data lives.

The five load-bearing equations

(3.8) — the grid. Fix the endpoints for robustness, then space the rest evenly:

p_i = a + (i − 1)/(k − 1) · (b − a),      i = 1, …, k

For k = 8 and (a, b) = (0.05, 0.95) that is [0.05, 0.178571, 0.307143, 0.435714, 0.564286, 0.692857, 0.821429, 0.95]. The three trims the thesis reports are (0.02, 0.98), (0.05, 0.95) and (0.10, 0.90).

(2.1) — the quantile covariance (Serfling's Theorem B). The empirical quantile vector is asymptotically normal about the true quantiles with covariance σ_ij / n:

σ_ij = p_i (1 − p_j) / [ f(F⁻¹(p_i)) · f(F⁻¹(p_j)) ]   for i ≤ j,   σ_ij = σ_ji otherwise

Two facts make this usable. First, once the family is fixed, replacing f, F⁻¹ by the standard f★, F★⁻¹ removes every unknown — Σ★ becomes a matrix of pure numbers. Second, for a log-location-scale family the Jacobian of the log transform is diagonal with entries 1/F⁻¹(p_i), and the F⁻¹(p_i)F⁻¹(p_j) factors cancel exactly against the matching factors in the numerator. The log family inherits the very same Σ★. That cancellation is the reason six different loss laws share one piece of code.

(3.4) / (3.6) — the two estimators. With Y = Xβ + ε, ε ~ AN(0, σ²Σ★/n):

oQLS:   β̂ = (X′X)⁻¹ X′Y                  — pretends Σ★ = I_k
gQLS:   β̂ = (X′Σ★⁻¹X)⁻¹ X′Σ★⁻¹Y           — uses the known Σ★

Numerically, never form Σ★⁻¹. Factor Σ★ = LL′ and run OLS on the whitened system L⁻¹X, L⁻¹Y — mathematically identical, numerically far safer. Σ★'s condition number runs from about 35 for the normal member at k = 8, (0.05, 0.95) up to 2.7e4 for log-Cauchy across the reported trims, and grows sharply as a → 0. Section 6 shows the implementation logging that condition number on every fit rather than hiding it.

(5.2) — in-sample goodness of fit. The gQLS residuals support a quadratic form that decomposes orthogonally, leaving

W = (n / σ̂²_gQLS) · (Y − Xβ̂)′ Σ★⁻¹ (Y − Xβ̂)   ~   χ²_{k−2}   under H₀

Here k = 8, so W ~ χ²₆ and the p-value is P(χ²₆ > W). This is the guardrail the decision track uses. One detail matters enormously for this data: an earlier test of the same shape estimated σ² by the sample variance, which requires a finite second moment. Equation (5.2) uses σ̂²_gQLS instead and therefore survives Cauchy-type tails — a small change with large consequences here, where the best-fitting family has no moments at all.

(5.3) — out-of-sample goodness of fit. W has a structural flaw for model comparison: it scores residuals only on the estimation grid, so a more aggressive trim shrinks the very interval being scored and looks better for free. The fix is a universal grid of r = 25 levels spanning 0.01 to 0.99, the same for every (a, b), giving W_out with β̂ still taken from the estimation grid. Because the two grids overlap only partially, the thesis calls the null distribution “a major challenge” and prices the p-value by parametric bootstrap (B = 1000). This study implements both that bootstrap and a naive χ²_{r−2} = χ²₂₃ reference, because RQ2 asks whether the expensive one earns its keep. Section 4 reports what happened, and it is more interesting than either registered answer.

(2.4) / (2.5) — why it is robust, formally. The influence function of each sample quantile is a bounded step function, and both estimators are fixed linear maps applied to that bounded vector. Boundedness is what “one bad record cannot move it far” means; positivity of BP is what “several bad records still cannot” means. They are different guarantees, and this study tests both — contamination for the first (RQ3), deletion for the second (RQ4). Section 5 shows the distinction turning out to matter far more than expected.

The log-location-scale unification — and Pareto I's disguise

A law is log-location-scale when log X is location-scale:

F⁻¹(u) = exp( μ + σ F★⁻¹(u) )    so    log F⁻¹(u) = μ + σ F★⁻¹(u)

— linear in the parameters, which is the entire reason a closed-form regression exists. Six families become one code path with six (f★, F★⁻¹) pairs: log-Cauchy tan(π(u − 0.5)), log-Gumbel −log(−log u), log-Laplace, log-Logistic −log(1/u − 1), lognormal Φ⁻¹(u), and Pareto I −log(1 − u).

Pareto I is the one worth staring at. Written the usual way — S(x) = (θ/x)^α, x > θ — it looks nothing like a location-scale law. Reparametrize μ = log θ, σ = 1/α and log X becomes a two-parameter exponential. Three consequences, all load-bearing:

  1. Its Q-Q plot is against standard exponential quantiles — which is why the bottom-right panel above looks anomalous next to the five symmetric ones.
  2. μ is not a centre; it is the left boundary of the support. Its MLE is the boundary estimator μ̂ = min(x), and σ̂ = mean(x) − min(x).
  3. Because μ̂ depends only on the minimum, Pareto I's MLE is perfectly insensitive to a contaminated maximum. Section 5 records the sealed grid confirming this to the digit: μ̂ = 21.541282 unchanged, σ̂ moving 1.258900 → 1.335653, which is exactly log(10)/30 = 0.076753. Robustness by accident of parametrization — predicted at the method gate, produced by the sealed run.

The catch this study exists to expose

Everything above is about parameters. An actuary does not sell a parameter; they sell a number like “the 1-in-100 event loss.” Getting from one to the other means pushing the estimate through the quantile transform

return level = exp( μ̂ + σ̂ · F★⁻¹(0.99) )

and that transform is not gentle. For the lognormal, F★⁻¹(0.99) = 2.326. For log-Cauchy — the family that fits this data best — F★⁻¹(0.99) = tan(0.49π) = 31.82. A 13.7× amplifier sitting in an exponent. The same 0.04 wobble in σ̂ moves a lognormal return level by about 10% and a log-Cauchy return level by a factor of 3.6.

So the method's headline claim (“robust parameters”) and the decision-maker's actual question (“stable 1-in-100”) can come apart — and they may come apart worst for the best-fitting model. That is RQ5 and RQ6, and it was genuinely open when the loop began.

The floors that govern every comparison in this report

Klein forbids guessing a minimum_delta. Phase adaptive-1 measured the floors before any comparison was allowed. Cite these; never re-derive them.

FloorValueWhat it governs
numerical (solver-route)8.8e−17 Nothing — and recording ≈0 is the finding. The arithmetic is exact to machine precision, so every disagreement with the published tables is a modeling choice, not a numerical artefact.
reporting resolution0.005 The reproduction track's minimum_delta: half the last published digit. This is what “reproduces” means on this track.
quantile-convention spread (k = 5 sidecar)0.018498 range (std 0.00664603) 3.7× the resolution — a specification spread, deliberately not folded into minimum_delta because it becomes constant once a kept candidate fixes the convention. Reported, not hidden.
paired log-return-level bootstrap SE3.461 (block spread 0.104) The decision track's stated uncertainty band. 3.59 of it comes from the log-Cauchy arm alone; its literal 2×SE on the return-level scale exceeds the metric's own range.

The fourth row deserves a second read, because it is where the study's punchline arrives early and in disguise. A bootstrap standard error so large that twice it exceeds the range of the metric it measures is not a nuisance number — it is a statement that at n = 30 the log-Cauchy 1-in-100 is not estimable to useful precision. The metrology knew RQ5's answer before the ranking did. What the loop added was the mechanism.

The Data

Thirty rows. That is the entire dataset, and it is not a sample of a bigger file — 30 rows is the dataset. Pielke & Landsea (1998), Table 8, “Top 30 Damaging Hurricanes,” each loss normalized to 1995 dollars for inflation, personal-property increase, and coastal-county population change. Transcribed from NOAA AOML/HRD, byte-verified against the data_hub source, and bundled inside the study directory so a bare clone reproduces every number.

The value-pattern check — and the trap that was not there

Klein's standing war story is that dtype == "object" is a lie: pandas string dtypes have silently broken that check before, so every column is audited by value, never by dtype. All eight columns were checked that way: 0 sentinels ("", NA, null, ?, -, unknown, -999, -1, 9999, nan all absent), 0 string-encoded booleans, 0 numbers-in-strings, 0 mixed-type columns, 0 duplicate rows.

The interesting result is a negative one. pre1925_flag is exactly the column shaped like the classic trap — a flag that a careless export would have written as "Yes"/"No" strings. Here it holds genuine integers 0/1, sums to 3, and its three set bits are exactly and only the three year < 1925 rows (set equality verified). Recording that the trap is absent is worth as much as catching it, because the next reader does not have to re-check.

Two more columns are exact by construction and were verified rather than assumed: damage_usd = damage_bn_1995 × 1e9 and log_damage_usd both reproduce to max|dev| 0.000e+00. The unit chain was pinned end-to-end because a millions-versus-billions misread is not silently survivable: mean(log_damage_usd) = 22.800182 equals the published MLE-lognormal μ̂ = 22.8002, and sd(ddof=0) = 0.833868 equals σ̂ = 0.8339. A misread would have placed μ̂ at 15.8924, off by log(1000) = 6.9078.

Four of eight columns are the target in disguise

The leakage audit — run clean-room, in a fresh context, from study.yaml, prepare.py, the prepared artifact and the estimator module only — returned 7/7 mechanized checks clean. But it flagged something that would be fatal in a different study:

rank is a deterministic bijection of the target: rank == 31 − rankdata(damage) exactly, Spearman −1.000000. So are damage_usd and log_damage_usd. Four of eight columns are the target under different encodings.

Why that is a non-issue here. This is univariate loss-model fitting. There is no feature matrix, no design matrix over covariates, and nothing to predict damage from; the estimators consume log_damage_usd as a sample, via sorted order statistics and a quantile grid. rank is precisely that sort order, so it carries no information the sample does not already contain. Why it must nevertheless be a standing rule: any model that regressed damage on rank would recover an identity (R² = 1) and report a triumphant, meaningless fit. The rule adopted at the data gate and honoured throughout: only log_damage_usd is consumed, and only as the sample being fitted.

The three WARNs — properties of the research object, not defects to fix

No BLOCKERs. Three WARNs, each carried verbatim into the findings and into this report, because each one constrains what may be said rather than what may be run.

WARN 1 — n = 30, and one observation dominates every tail fit

“max = 72.303 is 2.185× the second-largest (33.094) … Parametric bootstrap at n = 30 puts σ̂ = 0.8339 in a 95% interval of [0.617, 1.034] — a ±25% relative sampling band on the single parameter that drives the tail.”

That single observation is 20.5% of total damage mass; the top three are 37.5%. Deleting the maximum alone moves the mean −17.8% and the sd −44.7%. The consequence for this report is a wording rule, stated in the data card and repeated wherever it can erode: the declared 1.0 pp minimum_delta is “far smaller than the ±25% band on the estimand — treat it as an ordering device between estimators on a fixed sample, never as a claim about the population.”

WARN 2 — the decision functional is out-of-sample by construction

“The largest of 30 sits at plotting position p = 0.9667 ≈ 1-in-30. Every 1-in-100 quantile is therefore pure parametric extrapolation … the fitted lognormal 1-in-100 (55.52 bn) is below the largest observation actually seen (72.303 bn) — the ‘100-year loss’ is an artifact of the assumed family, not a data-supported number.”

Sit with that sentence. The number a committee would act on is smaller than an event that has already happened, and that is not a bug in the fit — it is what a lognormal tail implies given these thirty points. The prescribed action was to word every return-level claim as family-conditional and report the GoF-passing families side by side with the empirical 1-in-30 anchor, never a single number as “the” answer. Section 5 does exactly that, and the spread across four fits that all pass the same goodness-of-fit test spans nearly six orders of magnitude.

WARN 3 — the sealed evidence is independent TARGETS, not independent DATA

“the same 30 observations underlie both the adaptive and the sealed evaluation … it establishes implementation fidelity + within-sample robustness, never out-of-sample generalization. Sampling error is fully common-mode between adaptive and sealed evaluation and the sealed test cannot detect it.”

The audit's own assessment was even-handed and is worth quoting in both directions. Strength: the targets are third-party numbers fixed in print before this study existed, unmovable by anything the study does, and adaptively unoverfittable because the contract confined adaptive work to Table 6.9 while the sealed target is Table 6.10 — a stronger anti-peeking guarantee than a random fold, which an analyst can in principle inspect. Weakness: if these 30 draws are unrepresentative, the adaptive and sealed evaluations are wrong together, identically, and the sealed test is blind to it. A residual soft coupling also remains — a specification tuned until it hits Table 6.9 has thereby made much of Table 6.10 predictable — which the design bounds but does not eliminate.

Two NOTEs that turned into findings

The “1925–1995” period label is a mislabel — and it is load-bearing. Three rows fall outside that window: rank 3 (1900 Galveston, 26.619), rank 4 (1915 Galveston, 22.602) and rank 22 (1919 S Texas, 5.368). They are 15.5% of total damage and two of them are the #3 and #4 largest events in the sample. The published Table 6.8 statistics reproduce only with them included — which is exactly why R's extRemes::damage top-30, a genuinely 1925–95 set, does not reproduce the thesis. A replicator who “fixes” the period silently breaks the reproduction. pre1925_flag identifies the three rows exactly, and prepare.py's identity gate makes substituting the wrong 30-row set impossible to miss.

Two quantile conventions coexist in one thesis chapter. The data card flagged this as a live methodological sensitivity, not a data defect, before any model ran — and it is the seed of the whole detective story in section 4. The descriptive Table 6.8 quartiles (q1 = 4.0560, q3 = 12.4340) reproduce only under Hazen plotting positions; every alternative misses (normal_unbiased 0.0851, median_unbiased 0.1134, linear 0.3280, weibull 0.3402, inverted_cdf 0.6195). But the thesis's Chapter 2 defines the estimator's empirical quantile as F̂⁻¹(p) = X_(⌈np⌉) — NumPy's inverted_cdf. The card's verdict: Hazen for the descriptive table, ⌈np⌉ for the estimators, exported as two separately named constants so the two can never be confused.

The identity gate — what plays the role of a chance-level probe

With no partition and no predictor, the usual eval-harness sanity checks (constant and shuffled predictors scoring at chance) are inapplicable. What replaces them is a data-identity gate that prepare.py runs and that train.py re-verifies on every single run before any fitting happens. It checks 8 published Table-6.8 statistics plus 4 MLE-anchor scalars — 12 quantities — and it was re-run live for the audit:

n 0.00e+00 · min 0.00e+00 · q1 0.00e+00 · q2 8.88e-16 · q3 0.00e+00
max 0.00e+00 · mean 3.33e-05 · std_dev 2.82e-05
mle_lognormal_original    μ 22.8002 / σ 0.8339   — both exact at 0.00e+00
mle_lognormal_modified    μ 22.8769 / σ 1.0975   — both exact at 0.00e+00

That single gate pins four things at once: the sample (this is the AOML Table 8 top-30, not extRemes::damage and not the annual aggregate series), the period trap, the quantile convention used for the descriptive table, and the ×1e9 unit chain. Everything downstream rests on it, which is why section 6 argues it belongs inside the per-run code path rather than in a one-off setup script.

The Journey

Eleven ledger rows across two tracks and four phases. Every candidate was committed before it ran, so discards and crashes stay exactly as resolvable as keeps — negative evidence is evidence. Total measured compute for the entire study, all four phases: 7.7 seconds. Every fit is a two-parameter least-squares solve on eight points.

Two tracks, two frontiers

Each track's development frontier is a step function of keeps; discards sit off it as retained evidence; the purple star is that track's single sealed final-test access, drawn deliberately off the frontier because sealed evidence is excluded from adaptive selection.

adaptive-1 — an honest discard that asked the right question

Nothing may be compared before the ruler is calibrated. E0001 did two jobs: prove the pipeline is looking at the thesis's sample, and fit one single cell — gQLS lognormal at (0.05, 0.95) — against the published 22.79/0.82.

Both halves passed. The run was still discarded. The identity gate verified 12 quantities at max |dev| 3.53e-05; the single cell landed inside the 0.005 resolution (μ̂ 22.788710, σ̂ 0.824890, worst parameter deviation 0.004890). But the max_abs_w_deviation guardrail came in at 0.4940 against a limit of 0.10, and max_abs_p_deviation at 0.059404 against 0.02. The parameters matched and the goodness-of-fit statistic did not.

That is not a contradiction — it is a diagnostic. W is a quadratic form in the residuals, so it is far more sensitive to the exact position of the eight grid points than a two-parameter regression line through them is. A discard that fails on the sensitive quantity while passing on the insensitive one is telling you the grid itself is slightly wrong. The registered default convention was hazen — because that is what the data-identity gate demanded. The guardrail had just said it could not also be what the estimators use.

The same phase measured the floors: the numerical floor at 8.8e−17 (recording ≈0 is the finding), the k = 5 quantile-convention sweep at a spread of 0.018498 = 3.7× the resolution, and the decision track's paired log-return-level bootstrap SE at 3.461 — of which 3.59 comes from the log-Cauchy arm alone.

adaptive-2 — the convention, as a detective story

This is the part worth reading slowly, because it is a reproduction failure that turned into the study's most transferable finding.

The first clue: a table that fit too well. Before any modeling, the data card had noted that Table 6.8's descriptive quartiles reproduce only under Hazen plotting positions — MATLAB's quantile default — and under nothing else, by margins up to 0.62. A descriptive table that matches one convention exactly is not a coincidence; it silently identifies the software that produced it. So the study registered hazen as its default. That was the right call on the evidence available, and it was wrong.

The second clue: a guardrail breach that would not go away. E0001's W deviation of 0.4940 was the first warning. E0002 scaled the same convention to the full 18-cell grid and the problem scaled with it: mean 0.009303 — passing the mean prediction — but max_abs_param_deviation 0.031279, breaching the 0.02 guardrail outright, with max |ΔW| at 1.2855 and max |Δp| at 0.15813. Only 13 of 36 parameters were inside the resolution. The descriptive convention cannot reproduce the estimation tables. Recorded as a predicted discard, not a surprise — the prediction was written into the candidate description before the run.

The resolution: the thesis had already answered. Not in its results, in its definitions. Chapter 2's opening paragraph defines the empirical quantile as F̂⁻¹(p) = X_(⌈np⌉) — NumPy's inverted_cdf. The descriptive table was produced by one piece of software; the estimators were specified by the mathematics. Both statements are in the same chapter, and neither says the other exists.

E0003 changed one configuration line — CONVENTION = "inverted_cdf" — and the track's only KEEP landed:

QuantityE0002 (hazen)E0003 (inverted_cdf)Limit
mean |Δθ| over 36 parameters0.0093030.002754 = 0.55× the resolution0.005 (minimum_delta)
max |Δθ|0.031279 — BREACH0.0186870.02
max |ΔW|1.2855 — BREACH0.0050070.10
max |Δp|0.15813 — BREACH0.0048570.02
parameters inside resolution13 / 3635 / 36—

The mechanism, stated so it generalizes. At n = 3,000 the nine NumPy quantile conventions agree to four decimals and nobody notices. At n = 30 they disagree in the second decimal — which is exactly the decimal a paper reporting 22.79 / 0.82 is claiming. The convention sweep measured the whole spread on the track metric: inverted_cdf 0.002754 · hazen 0.009303 · normal_unbiased 0.011024 · median_unbiased 0.012036 · weibull 0.021252. Only one of the five lands inside the resolution the paper prints at.

The one cell that missed — and how the max guardrail earned its keep

The single over-resolution parameter of 36 is the (0.10, 0.90) log-Gumbel μ̂. Table 6.9 prints 22.34; our fit gives 22.358687, a deviation of 0.018687 — inside the 0.02 guardrail, but 3.7× the resolution.

The discriminating evidence is internal to the thesis. Table 6.10's g3 column prints 22.36 for the same fit — 0.0013 away from ours. So the reproduction does not disagree with the thesis; it disagrees with one printing of the thesis and agrees with the other. The study's own ledger records the verdict as a named aux metric: gumbel_g3_typo_verdict = table_6_9_is_the_typo.

Why this is worth a paragraph. A replicator without a max-deviation guardrail would never have seen it. That cell moves the mean by 0.0005 — one tenth of the resolution — so it would have been averaged away without a trace. The guardrail that exists to “stop one broken cell hiding behind a good average” earned its keep on a cell that turned out not to be a bug at all. Both outcomes are wins: if it had been our bug, the guardrail catches it; because it was not, the guardrail produced a small, citable correction to the published record.

E0004 — the p-values that were too good to be a bootstrap

RQ2 asked a cost question: the thesis prescribes a B = 1000 parametric bootstrap for the W_out p-value, which is expensive; is a plain χ²₂₃ reference indistinguishable? E0004 implemented both honestly (r = 25, B = 1000, seed 20260731) and returned two measurements that pull in opposite directions.

  1. The bootstrap is not numerically redundant. Our honest bootstrap departs from the χ²₂₃ reference by mean 0.0814 and max 0.2869 across the 18 cells — far beyond the registered 0.02 tolerance. The registered prediction is falsified.
  2. And yet 16 of 18 published p-values sit within 0.005 of the χ² reference — tighter than a B = 1000 bootstrap's own Monte-Carlo standard error (≈0.016 near p = 0.5) can be. Agreement that tight is not something a bootstrap can produce.

The two divergent cells are (0.02, 0.98) log-Logistic, which prints 0.16 against a χ² reference of 0.5939 (our bootstrap: 0.534), and (0.10, 0.90) log-Laplace, printing 0.55 against 0.4496 (our bootstrap: 0.486).

Wording discipline, applied deliberately. This is an observation about the reproducibility of printed numbers and nothing more. The published W_out statistics reproduce essentially exactly — 20.7905 against a printed 20.79, 23.1927 against 23.19 — so the fits and the test statistic are reproduced. It is only the route from statistic to p-value that cannot be reconstructed from the text as prescribed. Section 7 turns it into a one-sentence question for the author rather than an erratum.

E0005 — the Σ★ falsifier, the study's hardest gate

A wrong Σ★ fails silently. It still produces a fit, still produces plausible parameters, and nothing in the arithmetic complains. The pre-registered falsifier was therefore a specific number, with a STOP attached: reproduce the log-Cauchy σ̂ split between ordinary and generalized QLS — published as 0.23 versus 0.49 — or declare the covariance mis-specified and halt the study.

QuantityOursPublishedDeviation
o2 log-Cauchy σ̂ (ordinary QLS, (0.05, 0.95))0.2299120.238.84e−05
g2 log-Cauchy σ̂ (generalized QLS, same trim)0.4850550.490.004945
ratio g2/o22.10972.1304—

Passed exactly. Whole-arm means against the Table 6.10 originals: o2 0.0019355, o3 0.0014666, g2 0.0025893, g3 0.0019513, MLE 0.0021359. The closed-form covariance built from Serfling's theorem — written down before any data was seen — reproduces a published 2.11× efficiency split on real data. That is the moment the implementation became trustworthy.

The same phase ran an off-ledger k-sensitivity measurement, recorded in program.md and flagged in the findings as descriptive evidence with no run manifest. It refuted both halves of its registered prediction: parameters move by 0.1223 across k ∈ {8, 10, 15, 25} and 0.1040 across six conventions — 24.5× and 20.8× the reporting resolution. k moves things more than the convention does, and neither is a nuisance. The thesis pins k = 8 with inverted_cdf; under that pin, reproduction is exact.

adaptive-3 — from parameters to decisions

The reproduction track had answered its questions. The decision track now asked the one nobody had answered: among models that FIT, which gives the most stable 1-in-100? Four runs, each a different rung.

RunConfigurationW pClean 1-in-100InstabilityDisposition
E0006MLE-lognormal, no trim — the incumbent of practice0.5374$55.52bn58.06keep (baseline)
E0007gQLS log-Cauchy (0.05, 0.95) — the best-fitting family0.81764.08e7 $bn62.94discard
E0008gQLS lognormal (0.05, 0.95) — bounded transform0.5153$53.04bn41.33keep
E0009gQLS lognormal (0.10, 0.90) — the widest trim0.7310$56.66bn27.58keep — incumbent

E0006 set the baseline and already falsified one registered prediction: leave-top-1-out alone moves the MLE 1-in-100 by −25.68% (55.522 → 41.263 $bn), not the predicted >40%. The >40% level is first reached at leave-top-3 (−44.56%) and by 5× contamination (+58.06%), so the run-level metric held at 58.06 while the specific prediction did not.

E0007 is the study's punchline, and it arrived as a discard. The registered prediction was that gQLS log-Cauchy would be under ⅓ of MLE's instability — below 19.35. It came in at 62.94: 3.25× the predicted ceiling, and 1.08× the MLE baseline it was supposed to beat. The worst of the four contenders. Section 5 takes the refutation apart in three parts, because any one of them alone misleads.

E0008 isolated the mechanism by changing exactly one thing. Same estimator, same trim, same data, same GoF gate — only the family changes, log-Cauchy to lognormal, which changes only the standard quantile at p = 0.99 from 31.82 to 2.326. Instability: 62.94 → 41.33, a 21.62 pp move = 21.6× the ordering delta.

E0009 widened the trim from (0.05, 0.95) to (0.10, 0.90), raising the breakdown point from 0.05 to 0.10 — from “one bad record in thirty” to “three.” Instability fell again to 27.58, and the leave-top-1 stress collapsed from 19.02% to 5.66%. And the fit got better: W p rose from 0.5153 to 0.7310, matching the published 0.73 at that trim. The registered prediction had budgeted a goodness-of-fit cost for the wider trim; the cost came out negative.

Sealed confirmation — labelled separately, as it must be

Two runs, one per track, each spending that track's single sealed access against pre-registered published truth. Neither is on the adaptive frontier; both are excluded from selection by construction, which is why both appear as discard in the ledger despite being the study's strongest evidence.

E0010 — the full Table 6.10 grid (reproduction)

Five estimator arms × six families × original and 10×-modified data = 60 cells, 120 parameters that adaptive work never touched.

  • Mean |Δθ| 0.002026, max 0.005195, 119/120 inside the reporting resolution — better than the adaptive frontier, on four times as many parameters.
  • Every QLS arm's parameters are unchanged by the contamination, exactly. o2*, o3* and g3* are byte-identical to their unstarred twins (arm means 0.0019355 / 0.0014666 / 0.0019513 in both columns); g2* differs from g2 only through the published print (0.0026218 vs 0.0025893).
  • MLE moves as published. MLE*/lognormal reproduces at μ̂ 22.876935 (printed 22.88) and σ̂ 1.097494 (printed 1.10) against the clean 22.800182 / 0.833868 — a +31.6% move in σ̂ from one corrupted record in thirty.
  • The single over-resolution cell of 120 is g2*/log-Gumbel at 0.005195, and it is a printing artefact: our σ̂ = 0.734805 does not move under contamination, and Table 6.10 prints that same unchanged estimate as 0.73 in one column and 0.74 in the next — a last-digit rounding boundary.
  • A pleasing bonus the method card predicted in advance: Pareto I's contaminated σ̂ moves by exactly log(10)/30 = 0.076753 (1.258900 → 1.335653), with μ̂ = 21.541282 unchanged because its MLE is the boundary estimator min(x).

E0011 — the thesis's exact 10× modification (decision)

The incumbent from E0009 — gQLS lognormal at (0.10, 0.90) — run against the one contamination never used adaptively: 72.303 → 723.03. Adaptive stress had been capped at 5× precisely so that this 10× remained sealed.

Bit-identical. Not “within tolerance” — identical, because the trimmed quantile grid never reads the corrupted observation at all. The metric printed 0, and a metric of exactly zero is the rare case where the floor discussion is moot.

Paired with E0010's sealed MLE* parameters, that is the money number section 5 opens with: under the same single corrupted record, the incumbent of practice doubles and the study's incumbent does not move.

Findings

Start with the number a committee can act on.

Take one record out of thirty — the 1926 Great Miami hurricane at $72.303bn — and multiply it by ten, the way a decimal-point slip or a double-counted recovery does. On maximum likelihood with a lognormal, the fitted 1-in-100 event loss goes from $55.5bn to $110.7bn, +99.4%. On gQLS-lognormal at trim (0.10, 0.90), the same corruption produces $56.7bn → $56.7bn, 0.0% — bit-identical in μ̂, σ̂ and all three return levels.

Both halves of that pair are on-ledger and sealed. The 0.0% is E0011, the decision track's single sealed access, run against the thesis's exact modification. The +99.4% is formed from E0006's clean MLE fit (55.522182) and E0010's sealed MLE* parameters (μ̂ 22.876935, σ̂ 1.097494), which give 110.700 — derived on-ledger, never re-fitted for the page.
