Evidence-level discipline. C1 and C3 are confirmed because the reproduction track's single sealed access was spent on exactly those two questions, against 120 parameters the loop never touched. C6's incumbent statement is confirmed by the decision track's single access; its general “iff bounded transform” form, and the whole of C4 and C5, remain development-stress comparisons and stay exploratory. C2 is exploratory by construction — it is a statement about published p-values, not about a frontier. Nothing here is a population claim.

The RQ5 punchline, in three parts that must be quoted together

gQLS log-Cauchy is the family the thesis's own goodness-of-fit test ranks first on this data (W p = 0.8176, the highest of six). Here is what it does. Quote any one of these alone and you will mislead someone:

#MeasurementWhat it says on its own
i 0.0% contamination movement. Inflate the largest loss 5× (or 10×) and the parameters do not move at all. “Perfect robustness.” True, and the trim genuinely never reads the corrupted point.
ii 62.94% resample instability. Delete the top observation and the 1-in-100 moves 62.94%; at k = 2, 47.21%; at k = 3, 61.32%. “The worst of the four contenders” — worse than the untrimmed MLE it was supposed to beat.
iii A clean 1-in-100 of 4.08e7 $bn (≈ $4.1e16) — about 5.6e5× the largest event ever recorded — because tan(0.49π) = 31.82 multiplies σ̂ in the exponent. “The level is meaningless.” And it passes every diagnostic an analyst would normally run.

The mechanism — why (i) and (ii) are not a contradiction. The two stresses act through different channels. Inflation changes a value the trimmed grid never reads, so nothing propagates: the influence function is bounded and the breakdown point does its job. Deletion changes which order statistics the fixed probability levels land on — the estimator is asked for the same probability levels of a genuinely different sample — so σ̂ moves a little. And then tan(0.49π) = 31.82 sits in the exponent and turns “a little” into a factor: a 0.04 move in σ̂ multiplies the return level by about 3.6.

Robust-to-outliers ≠ robust-to-resampling. A bounded influence function protects the parameters; only a bounded quantile transform protects the decision. That sentence is the study's single most transferable result.

And the metrology said it first. The decision track's paired log-return-level bootstrap SE is 3.461, of which 3.59 comes from the log-Cauchy arm alone — a standard error whose literal 2× on the return-level scale exceeds the metric's own range. At n = 30 this family's 1-in-100 is not estimable to useful precision, and the floor sweep in adaptive-1 knew that before the ranking in adaptive-3 confirmed it.

One consequence the code enforces rather than documents. log-Cauchy has no finite moments. In this study's implementation mean_loss() and cte() raise NotImplementedError by design. A numerical CTE would return a large float that is an artefact of where the quadrature was truncated and would look exactly like an estimate. An actuary who follows the goodness-of-fit test into a TVaR-loaded premium gets a confident number with no meaning; the refusal converts a silent pricing error into a stack trace.

The breakdown-point ladder

Read the solid line first: 58.06 → 41.33 → 27.58 as the breakdown point goes 0 → 0.05 → 0.10. Monotone, and the total move of 30.479351 pp is 30.5× the ordering delta. Now read the dashed line: on deletion alone it is 44.56 → 41.33 → 27.58. The MLE's binding stress is contamination; for gQLS, contamination is free and deletion is the whole cost.

The most striking rung is the leave-top-1 stress specifically, which collapses 19.02% → 5.66% between the two trims. Widening the trim by five percentage points at each end cut the single most likely real-world perturbation by more than two-thirds.

Why the cliff is missing, and why that is informative. The registered prediction was that k = 2 (2/30 = 0.067, past BP = 0.05) would breach the narrow trim. It cost only +3.70 pp relative to the wider trim. The reason is that BP = min{a, 1−b} guarantees an estimate cannot be driven arbitrarily by corruption in place — and deletion is a different stress, because dropping the top k re-indexes every order statistic. The cliff-shaped guarantee shows up on the stress BP actually governs: under 5× inflation of the maximum, both gQLS trims sit at exactly 0.0% while the MLE moves +58.06%.

And the trim was free here. Prediction 8 budgeted a goodness-of-fit cost for the wider trim. Instead W p rose from 0.5153 to 0.7310 (matching the published 0.73). The mechanism: W is scored only on the estimation grid, so a wider trim scores a wider interval — the very structural flaw the universal W_out grid exists to fix — and the extreme levels a narrow trim reaches are precisely where a 30-point sample is noisiest. Check this on your own data rather than assuming it: the classical efficiency argument says a wider trim must cost fit, and on this sample it did not.

Surprises

  1. The thesis uses two different quantile conventions in one chapter, and never says so. Section 4 tells it as a detective story. The generalizable form is C7 in section 6: a gQLS specification is five things — (family, a, b, k, quantile convention) — and the last two are usually left to a library default.
  2. The reproduction localized a typo in the published table — and proved it was a typo. Table 6.9's (0.10, 0.90) log-Gumbel μ̂ prints 22.34; our fit gives 22.358687; Table 6.10 prints 22.36 for the same fit, 0.0013 from ours. The reproduction does not disagree with the thesis — it disagrees with one printing and agrees with the other.
  3. The published p-values are too close to a χ² reference to have come from the prescribed bootstrap. 16 of 18 within 0.005, when a B=1000 bootstrap's own MC standard error near p = 0.5 is ≈0.016 and our honest bootstrap wanders from χ² by mean 0.0814. Agreement that tight is not something a bootstrap can produce. Stated as a reproducibility observation about printed numbers, and sent to section 7 as a question rather than an erratum.
  4. The best-fitting family is perfectly contamination-robust and catastrophically resample-unstable at the same time — 0.0% and 62.94% from the same fit. Detailed above; it is the study's headline.
  5. k moves the estimates more than the convention does, and both are ~20× the reporting resolution. Max parameter movement 0.1223 across k ∈ {8, 10, 15, 25} versus 0.1040 across six conventions. The mechanism: at n = 30, asking for k = 25 distinct quantile levels on (0.05, 0.95) requests more resolution than 30 order statistics contain — levels collapse onto repeated order statistics and the design matrix starts describing ties rather than the distribution. (The measurement reports the k ≤ 15 restriction separately and it is the same 0.1223, so this is not a k = 25 artefact.)
  6. Widening the trim made the in-sample fit better, not worse — and one “over-resolution” sealed cell turned out to be a rounding boundary (g2*/log-Gumbel: our unchanged σ̂ = 0.734805 printed as 0.73 in one column and 0.74 in the next). Two different reproduction “failures”, both resolved by looking at what was typeset. A pleasing confirmation in the same grid: Pareto I's contaminated σ̂ moves by exactly log(10)/30 = 0.076753, with μ̂ unchanged because its MLE is the boundary estimator — the method card predicted the number before the sealed run produced it.

What it is worth

The value proposition as one number a committee can act on: the difference between the two methods is a doubling of the modelled 100-year loss, caused by one bad row that no data-quality process caught. For a catastrophe layer, a capital charge, or a solvency return, a 100% error in the 1-in-100 is not a modelling nuance; it is the difference between two different companies. Quantile trimming is, in this specific and quantifiable sense, data-quality insurance: it costs a defined amount of statistical efficiency and it pays out exactly when a record is wrong.

And the honest version is more useful than the inflated one. The +99.4% and the 0.0% are properties of this fixed 30-event sample under this stress. σ̂ carries a ±25% bootstrap band at n = 30, and the 1.0 pp minimum_delta is an ordering device, not a confidence statement. What transfers is not “gQLS gives you a 0.0% number”; it is the structure — an estimator that never reads the corrupted observation cannot be moved by it, and an estimator that reads every observation can be moved arbitrarily. The first is a theorem; the second is arithmetic. The sizing on your own book is a measurement you must repeat.

The counter-lesson costs more to learn the hard way. The best-fitting family by the thesis's own test produces a 1-in-100 of $4.08e7bn — roughly 400× world GDP — while passing every diagnostic an analyst would normally run and being perfectly robust at the parameter level. An analyst who selects a severity family by GoF p-value and quotes its 1-in-100 has done everything the textbook asks and produced a number with no economic content. Three cheap guardrails would have caught it: refuse moments on moment-free families; print the return level next to the empirical maximum; and treat any extrapolation more than an order of magnitude beyond observed support as a modelling failure rather than a tail estimate. The GoF test answers “does this shape fit the middle of my data”; it does not answer “is the tail I am about to sell defensible”.

Adoption economics. A method published in an August 2024 dissertation was implemented from scratch (six families, two estimators, two goodness-of-fit tests, a parametric bootstrap), validated against 156 published parameters (36 adaptive + 120 sealed) to a mean deviation of about 0.002, stressed beyond anything the source publishes, carried into the decision unit the source explicitly names as future work, and closed with a full audit trail — inside one session and 11 experiments, with total measured compute of 7.7 seconds. The transferable claim is not that gQLS is cheap to run. It is that the evaluation of a frontier method is now cheap enough that “we don't know if it works on our data” has stopped being a reason to defer it. The binding constraint is whether anyone writes down, in advance, what would have to be true for the method to be rejected. That is what the eight registered predictions and the two sealed accesses bought — and three of the eight came back refuted, including the one the study existed to ask.

Limitations

Carried in the spirit of the data card's own wording rules, which were written before any modeling and are quoted where they are load-bearing.

  1. n = 30, and one observation dominates every tail fit. “max = 72.303 is 2.185× the second-largest (33.094) … Parametric bootstrap at n = 30 puts σ̂ = 0.8339 in a 95% interval of [0.617, 1.034] — a ±25% relative sampling band on the single parameter that drives the tail.” Consequently the 1.0 pp minimum_delta is “far smaller than the ±25% band on the estimand — treat it as an ordering device between estimators on a fixed sample, never as a claim about the population.” Every decision-track number above is such an ordering.
  2. The decision functional is out-of-sample by construction. “The largest of 30 sits at plotting position p = 0.9667 ≈ 1-in-30. Every 1-in-100 quantile is therefore pure parametric extrapolation … the fitted lognormal 1-in-100 (55.52 bn) is below the largest observation actually seen (72.303 bn) — the ‘100-year loss’ is an artifact of the assumed family, not a data-supported number.” The four GoF-passing 1-in-100s here span nearly six orders of magnitude — $53.04bn, $55.52bn, $56.66bn and $4.08e7bn — on the same data.
  3. The sealed evidence is independent TARGETS, not independent DATA. “the same 30 observations underlie both the adaptive and the sealed evaluation … it establishes implementation fidelity + within-sample robustness, never out-of-sample generalization. Sampling error is fully common-mode between adaptive and sealed evaluation and the sealed test cannot detect it.” A residual soft coupling also remains — a specification tuned until it hits Table 6.9 has thereby made much of Table 6.10 predictable — which the design bounds but does not eliminate.
  4. Stationarity is inherited, not established. The 30 events span 1900–1995 and are treated as exchangeable draws from one severity distribution solely because of the Pielke-Landsea normalization for inflation, wealth and coastal population. Anything that normalization fails to remove — building codes, warning lead times, insurance penetration, any trend in storm intensity — is absorbed silently into σ̂ and therefore into every return level here. The observed r(year, log damage) = −0.42 is equally consistent with sampling noise and with over-normalization, and cannot be distinguished at n = 30.
  5. The MLE baseline's GoF gate is heuristic. The w_pvalue ≥ 0.10 guardrail admitted E0006 on W p = 0.5374 with w_chi2_calibrated = 0: the χ²k−2 calibration is established for gQLS residuals and the implementation correctly flags that it is not established for an MLE fit. The MLE arm passed a comparable-looking screen rather than a calibrated one. This does not affect C5's ordering (log-Cauchy loses on its own calibrated fit), but the MLE row of any comparison table should carry the flag.
  6. The k-sensitivity result is off-ledger. It is a program.md-recorded measurement with no run manifest and no experiment-level uncertainty. It was re-verified at synthesis and reproduces exactly (0.12227960638 across k; 0.10393799264 across conventions), but it is descriptive evidence and no verdict rests on it alone.
  7. The playbook was never filled — and that is a process finding, not a footnote. All four of playbook.md's tables remained at their scaffolded headers, so the pre-clustered discard map the synthesis protocol expects to mine did not exist; the synthesis reconstructed the clusters from program.md's decision log and the ledgers instead. All three phase acknowledgements recorded the same (scaffold) hash, so the gap was visible in the audit trail rather than hidden by it. The record is silent on why, and nothing is inferred. Two things are worth saying about it. First, the reconstruction worked because the journal and the ledgers are append-only and complete — the redundancy in the protocol is what made a missing artifact recoverable rather than fatal. Second, a future study on this ladder should treat the playbook as load-bearing: the reconstruction cost real synthesis effort and, on a longer study with more discards, would not have been possible at the same fidelity. Reporting the gap is cheaper than the gap.
  8. Two GoF-passing families were never carried into the decision track. log-Logistic and log-Laplace pass comfortably (W p 0.5349 and 0.5965 at (0.05, 0.95)) and their standard quantiles at p = 0.99 are bounded (4.60 and 3.91), so they are plausible middle rungs between lognormal (2.326) and log-Cauchy (31.82). The adaptive-3 budget went to the trim ladder instead. C6's “iff bounded” is therefore supported by a two-point contrast, not by a curve.

Coding Advice

This is the section that makes the artifact useful. Below is the actual winning train.py, byte-for-byte as committed at E0009 — the configuration that produced the decision track's best frontier value (27.584597) and became the incumbent for the sealed run — followed by what it does that matters, and the traps that actually fired in this study.

The winning train.py, verbatim

"""The only per-candidate mutable surface in a Klein v2 study.

Study 06 — hurricane gQLS reproduction and return levels. Every computation lives in
`analysis.py` (the stable study library); this file selects ONE mode and its arguments,
re-verifies the data-identity anchor, and hands the result to the v2 evaluator.

Two tracks, two primary metric names — the printed name MUST match the track being run
or `klein run-one` refuses the result:

    KLEIN_TRACK=reproduction  ->  mean_abs_param_deviation      (lower)
    KLEIN_TRACK=decision      ->  return_level_instability_pct  (lower)

Guardrails are read by the runner off the PRINTED block, so `extra` carries every
guardrail key of the running track with its measured value — `analysis.check_extra`
asserts that before a mode may return (study 05, lesson F1). Guardrail `wall_seconds`
is added here, the only place that knows `t0`.

Sealed evidence: `sealed_repro` / `sealed_decision` read pre-registered published truth
(the full Table 6.10 grid; the exact 72.303 -> 723.03 modification) and may run ONLY
under `klein run-one --final-test`, once per track. The guard below is what enforces it.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import os
import time

import analysis

from kleinlib.eval import evaluate_scalar

SMOKE = os.environ.get("KLEIN_SMOKE") == "1"

# ---- CONFIG: the per-experiment surface (keep diffs 5-15 lines) ----
MODE = "decision"          # anchor | grid | gof_redundancy | oqls_mle_arms | sensitivity
                         # | decision | sealed_repro | sealed_decision
CONVENTION = "inverted_cdf"     # inverted_cdf | hazen | weibull | median_unbiased | normal_unbiased
K = 8                    # quantile levels per fit; Tables 6.9/6.10 use k = 8
ESTIMATOR = "gqls"
FAMILY = "lognormal"
TRIM = (0.10, 0.90)      # decision modes only: the (a, b) quantile trim
# -------------------------------------------------------------------

EXPERIMENT_ID = os.environ.get("KLEIN_EXPERIMENT_ID") or ("SMOKE" if SMOKE else None)
TRACK = os.environ.get("KLEIN_TRACK") or (
    analysis.MODE_TRACK.get(MODE) if SMOKE else None
)

DECISION_MODES = {"decision", "sealed_decision"}


def main() -> None:
    t0 = time.time()
    evaluation_kind = os.environ.get("KLEIN_EVALUATION_KIND") or (
        "development" if SMOKE else None
    )
    missing = [
        name
        for name, value in (
            ("KLEIN_EVALUATION_KIND", evaluation_kind),
            ("KLEIN_EXPERIMENT_ID", EXPERIMENT_ID),
            ("KLEIN_TRACK", TRACK),
        )
        if value is None
    ]
    if missing:
        raise RuntimeError(
            "train.py must be invoked through `klein run-one`. For a pre-run "
            "syntax/shape check use `KLEIN_SMOKE=1 python train.py` — it prints the "
            "canonical block, writes no sidecars or snapshots, and is not evidence. "
            "Missing: " + ", ".join(missing)
        )
    if evaluation_kind not in {"development", "final_test"}:
        raise RuntimeError(f"invalid KLEIN_EVALUATION_KIND={evaluation_kind!r}")

    # ---- contract checks: mode, track, and sealed access must agree ----
    if MODE not in analysis.MODES:
        raise RuntimeError(
            f"unknown MODE={MODE!r}; expected one of {sorted(analysis.MODES)}"
        )
    if TRACK not in analysis.TRACK_METRIC:
        raise RuntimeError(
            f"invalid KLEIN_TRACK={TRACK!r}; expected one of {sorted(analysis.TRACK_METRIC)}"
        )
    if analysis.MODE_TRACK[MODE] != TRACK:
        raise RuntimeError(
            f"MODE={MODE!r} belongs to track {analysis.MODE_TRACK[MODE]!r}, but this run "
            f"is on track {TRACK!r} — the primary metric name would not match the contract"
        )
    sealed = MODE in analysis.SEALED_MODES
    if evaluation_kind == "final_test" and not sealed:
        raise RuntimeError(
            f"--final-test spends a track's one sealed access, but MODE={MODE!r} is an "
            f"adaptive mode; sealed modes are {sorted(analysis.SEALED_MODES)}"
        )
    if sealed and evaluation_kind != "final_test":
        message = (
            f"MODE={MODE!r} reads PRE-REGISTERED SEALED evidence and must run through "
            "`klein run-one --final-test`, once per track"
        )
        if not SMOKE:
            raise RuntimeError(message)
        print(f"[smoke] {message} — shape check only, not evidence")

    # ---- data-identity anchor: re-verified on EVERY run, before any fitting ----
    identity = analysis.verify_identity()
    print(
        f"identity anchor OK: {identity['identity_stats_verified']} statistics, "
        f"max |deviation| {identity['identity_max_abs_deviation']:.2e}"
    )

    if MODE in DECISION_MODES:
        primary, extra = analysis.MODES[MODE](ESTIMATOR, FAMILY, TRIM, CONVENTION, K)
    else:
        primary, extra = analysis.MODES[MODE](CONVENTION, K)

    evaluate_scalar(
        primary,
        exp_id=EXPERIMENT_ID,
        metric_name=analysis.TRACK_METRIC[TRACK],
        metric_goal="lower",
        study_dir=".",
        t0=t0,
        extra={
            **extra,
            "wall_seconds": time.time() - t0,
            "mode": MODE,
            "convention": CONVENTION,
        },
    )


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Annotated: seven things this file does that matter

  1. The mutable surface is a nine-line CONFIG block, and nothing else. MODE, CONVENTION, K, ESTIMATOR, FAMILY, TRIM. Every computation lives in analysis.py, the stable study library. That is what made E0003 possible: the fix that turned a guardrail-breaching discard into the track's only KEEP was one word — hazen → inverted_cdf — and the diff proves nothing else changed. If the convention had been buried in the estimator module, the same fix would have been an unfalsifiable multi-line edit.
  2. It refuses to run outside the harness. The missing check demands KLEIN_EVALUATION_KIND, KLEIN_EXPERIMENT_ID and KLEIN_TRACK from the environment and raises with the exact remedy (KLEIN_SMOKE=1 for a shape check) rather than defaulting. A train.py that “works” when run by hand is a train.py that will one day produce a number with no manifest behind it.
  3. Mode, track and metric name are cross-checked before any fitting. Two tracks mean two primary metric names, and klein run-one refuses a result whose printed metric name does not match the track being run. Rather than discover that after a run, analysis.MODE_TRACK[MODE] != TRACK raises immediately with a message naming both. This is cheap defensive code that pays for itself the first time you edit MODE and forget the --track flag.
  4. The sealed-mode guard is in the code, not in the discipline. sealed_repro and sealed_decision read pre-registered published truth and may only run under klein run-one --final-test. The file enforces both directions: a sealed mode without --final-test raises, and --final-test on an adaptive mode raises too (“--final-test spends a track's one sealed access”). A single sealed access per track is a contract you cannot un-spend, so the guard belongs where it cannot be forgotten.
  5. The data-identity anchor is re-verified on EVERY run, before any fitting. Twelve published quantities, checked in three lines — E0001's entire run, identity gate plus fit, took 2.2 ms. It is tempting to run this once in prepare.py and trust it thereafter. Don't: it is the only thing standing between this study and a silent substitution of extRemes::damage's genuinely-1925–95 top-30, which looks like the same dataset, is not, and would break every published comparison while raising no error. The gate is cheap; the failure it prevents is invisible.
  6. Guardrails are printed, not merely written. The runner reads guardrail values off the printed canonical block, so extra must carry every guardrail key of the running track with its measured value — analysis.check_extra asserts that before a mode may return, and wall_seconds is added here because this file is the only place that knows t0. This is study 05's lesson F1 imported as code: there, a metric that was written to aux_metrics.tsv but not printed cost a real experiment slot.
  7. The convention and the mode are recorded in extra on every run. "mode": MODE, "convention": CONVENTION — two strings that turn every ledger row into a self-describing record. When section 4's detective story needed to prove that E0002 and E0003 differed only in the convention, the evidence was already in aux_metrics.tsv; nobody had to reconstruct it from commit messages.

War stories — the traps that actually fired

Never form Σ★⁻¹ — factor and whiten

The textbook GLS formula β̂ = (X′Σ⁻¹X)⁻¹X′Σ⁻¹Y invites you to compute Σ★⁻¹. Do not. Σ★'s condition number runs to 2.7e4 for log-Cauchy across the reported trims (against about 35 for the normal member at k = 8, (0.05, 0.95)), and it grows sharply as a → 0; on the r = 25 validation grid it is far worse still, since the standard Cauchy density at the 0.01 quantile is ≈3e−4. The mathematically identical, numerically safe route is Cholesky whitening:

L = cholesky(Sig, lower=True)
mu, sigma = lstsq(solve_tri(L, X), solve_tri(L, Y))[0]

# and the GoF statistic uses the SAME factor - a squared norm, again no inverse
r = Y - X @ [mu, sigma]
W = n / sigma**2 * (solve_tri(L, r) ** 2).sum()

And log the condition number on every fit. The study's estimator returns sigma_star_cond with each gQLS result, so the loop can see conditioning degrade rather than infer it from a bad answer. E0002 and E0003 both recorded sigma_star_cond_max = 27302.62 on the log-Cauchy family — identical across the two conventions, which is itself evidence that the convention change moved the data vector and not the covariance.

Make the code refuse what the mathematics refuses

log-Cauchy has no finite moments. In this implementation, mean_loss() and cte() raise NotImplementedError for such families rather than returning a number. The ledger carries the reason as a first-class aux metric on E0007:

moment_note: “log-Cauchy has NO finite moments: mean_loss() and cte() raise NotImplementedError by design, so this family can only ever be priced through QUANTILES — any mean/CTE/TVaR number for it is a truncation artifact.”

This is the cheapest control in the study and the one most likely to matter in production. A numerical quadrature would have returned a large float that is an artefact of where it was truncated, and it would have looked exactly like an estimate. The refusal fires at the moment of misuse and converts a silent pricing error into a stack trace. Note the corollary: a moment-based robust estimator (trimmed or Winsorized moments) has nothing to trim on a family with no moments — which is precisely the gap the quantile grid fills.

Export both conventions under different names, so they can never be confused

This study needs two quantile conventions for two different jobs, and mixing them up costs a guardrail breach. The implementation exports them as separately named constants — SUMMARY_QUANTILE_METHOD (Hazen, for the descriptive identity gate) and THESIS_QUANTILE_METHOD (inverted_cdf, for the estimators) — and takes method= everywhere, so a pre-registered convention sweep is still possible. One further wrinkle is exposed as quantile_space=: the thesis writes Y = log F̂⁻¹(p) (quantile the dollars, then log), which is identical to quantiling the log-dollars under order-statistic conventions but not under interpolating ones.

A guardrail that fails while the metric passes is a signal, not a nuisance

E0001 produced parameters inside the reporting resolution and was discarded on a max_abs_w_deviation of 0.4940. The temptation in that moment is to widen the guardrail, because the headline number looked fine. The correct reading is that W is a quadratic form in the residuals and therefore far more sensitive to the exact grid than a two-parameter regression line through it — so the insensitive quantity passing while the sensitive one fails localizes the bug to the grid. That single discard is what sent the study back to Chapter 2's definition and produced its only reproduction KEEP.

Predict the disposition in the candidate description

Every candidate description in this study's ledger states the expected metric and the expected disposition before the run: E0002's says “predicted mean ~0.0093 with max_abs_param_deviation ~0.032 BREACHING the 0.02 guardrail … discard predicted”. Two benefits, both real. A prediction that lands makes the discard informative rather than disappointing — E0002 was a deliberate measurement of a convention, not a failed attempt. And a prediction that misses is caught immediately, while the reasoning is still in your head rather than three phases later.

Five transferable rules

  1. Pin the quantile convention AND k in any filing, paper, or model document whose parameters come from a quantile-based fit — and reproduce the source's descriptive table first to find out which convention it used. A gQLS specification is five things — (family, a, b, k, quantile convention) — and the last two are usually left to a library default. At n = 30 the convention alone moves a fitted parameter by up to 0.1040 and k by up to 0.1223: 20.8× and 24.5× the 0.005 reporting resolution. Swapping hazen for inverted_cdf is the whole difference between a discard at 0.009303 with a breached guardrail and a keep at 0.002754. (C7)
  2. Price a moment-free fit through quantiles only — and make the code refuse the rest. The best-fitting family on this data has no finite mean. An actuary who follows the goodness-of-fit test into a TVaR-loaded premium gets a confident number with no meaning; the NotImplementedError is the control. (C8)
  3. Treat the trim as the robustness knob, price it explicitly, and buy it before you need it. Moving from (0.05, 0.95) to (0.10, 0.90) cut 1-in-100 instability from 41.33 to 27.58 and raised the in-sample GoF from W p 0.5153 to 0.7310. The knob has a directly readable meaning: BP = min{a, 1−b} is the number of corrupted records you are buying protection against — 5% of 30 events is 1.5, so one bad record is tolerated and two are not; 10% tolerates three. Because the breakdown point is a guarantee with a cliff, not a slope, widen the trim while the sample is still clean; past the cliff there is no partial credit. And check the cost on your data: the classical efficiency argument says a wider trim must cost fit, and here it did not. (C9)
  4. State family-conditionality next to every return level, and anchor it to the empirical support. With n = 30 the largest observation sits at plotting position p = 0.9667 ≈ 1-in-30, so every 1-in-100 here is parametric extrapolation. The numbers make the point better than the caveat does: on the same data and the same estimator the 1-in-100 is $53.04bn (gQLS-lognormal 0.05/0.95), $56.66bn (gQLS-lognormal 0.10/0.90), $55.52bn (MLE-lognormal) and $4.08e7bn (gQLS log-Cauchy). All four pass the in-sample GoF test; three sit below the largest event actually observed and one sits five orders of magnitude above any loss in recorded history. Report the GoF-passing families side by side with the empirical 1-in-30 anchor, never a single number as “the” answer. (C10)
  5. When your “held-out” evidence is published targets rather than held-out data, say exactly that in the claim, not in a footnote. This study's sealed evidence is unusually strong on one axis — 120 third-party parameters fixed in print before the study existed, unmovable by anything the study does — and structurally blind on another: the same 30 observations underlie both evaluations, so sampling error is fully common-mode. The permitted claim is “our implementation reproduces their published numbers on their sample, and the estimator is robust within that sample”. The forbidden claim is any statement about generalization to another hurricane sample, another period, or predictive accuracy. Carry the wording verbatim into slides and verdict cards, where it is most likely to erode. (C11)

What the implementation cost

About 970 lines of numpy/scipy (estimators.py 802 + stress.py 171) covering six standard members, oQLS + gQLS + MLE, both goodness-of-fit tests and the B = 1000 parametric bootstrap, backed by 20/20 tests in 0.69 s. The mathematical core is about fifteen lines: grid → design matrix → known Σ★ → Cholesky-whitened least squares. There is no released R or Python package for gQLS — adoption means owning the code and its tests. Budget for the tests that pin your Σ★ specifically, because a wrong Σ★ fails silently and only the o2-versus-g2 split catches it.

Next Steps

Five follow-ups, each with a prediction that could falsify it. They are ordered by information per unit of effort, not by ambition.

1. Full-sample replication on extRemes::damage (n = 144)

The highest-information follow-up, and the one that converts every claim here from within-sample to out-of-sample. This study's structural limitation is that sealing gave independent targets and not independent data (limitation 3). R's extRemes::damage carries the complete Pielke-Landsea normalized series, not just the top 30 — a genuinely larger sample from the same generating process, on which the same estimators can be refitted and the same stresses re-run.

Predictions to falsify. (a) The gQLS→MLE efficiency gap becomes visible at n = 144, so the trim's cost stops being free — lever 8 came out the good way at n = 30 and should not at n = 144. (b) The convention and k sensitivities fall by roughly √(30/144) ≈ 0.46 in parameter units, testing the grid-resolution mechanism directly. (c) The log-Cauchy 1-in-100 stays economically absurd, because that is a property of the transform and not of the sample size.

Note the sample is not the thesis's — the identity gate will and should fail. This is a new study, not an extension of this ledger.

2. A GPD / peaks-over-threshold arm on the same data

The comparison an EVT reviewer asks for first. Every fit here is a full-sample log-location-scale law extrapolated to p = 0.99; the standard alternative models only exceedances over a threshold with a generalized Pareto tail and estimates the shape ξ rather than choosing it by family selection.

Prediction to falsify: a GPD tail fitted above the ~1-in-10 threshold gives a 1-in-100 within a factor of 2 of the gQLS-lognormal $56.66bn — i.e. the lognormal answer is the defensible one and log-Cauchy's is an artefact of forcing one family to describe both body and tail. If instead the GPD lands an order of magnitude higher, C10 strengthens sharply: family-conditionality is not a caveat but the dominant term. Pair it with robust GPD estimators so the comparison is robust-vs-robust rather than robust-vs-MLE.

3. Frequency × severity: the annual aggregate series and a compound model

The 1-in-100 event loss is not the 1-in-100 year — and the year is what a reinsurance programme or a capital model needs. The Pielke-Landsea data supports the annual aggregate series that Katz (2002) models as compound Poisson–lognormal.

Prediction to falsify: the annual-aggregate 1-in-100 is less sensitive to the single corrupted record than the per-event 1-in-100, because frequency uncertainty (a Poisson count over ~96 years) dominates severity uncertainty at the aggregate level. That would make the +99.4% headline an upper bound on what data quality costs a real capital number, and would mean C9's trim advice matters most for per-event layers.

4. Framework fix — per-track sealed-access maps should be topped up from the contract

klein new scaffolds one track and derives final_holdout_access keys at scaffold time; a second track added by editing study.yaml — still the only way to build a two-track study — leaves that map stale and the sealed run is refused. Study 05 lost a real experiment slot to it. This study avoided it only because a human remembered the lesson and hand-topped the map before Gate 0, which is a workaround, not a fix. Do: have load_state reconcile the map against the current contract, or let klein new accept repeated --track. Cheap, and it is now two studies deep.

5. Send the author one gentle question about the W_out p-value route

C2 and surprise 3 should reach the source as a question, not as an erratum. The W_out statistics reproduce to ≤0.005 across all 18 cells, and 16/18 p-values match a χ²₂₃ reference more closely than a B = 1000 bootstrap's own Monte-Carlo error permits, while the text prescribes the bootstrap. The useful message is one sentence — “could you confirm which reference distribution produced the Table 6.9 p-column, so that replicators can reproduce it?” — plus an offer of the two divergent cells ((0.02, 0.98) log-Logistic and (0.10, 0.90) log-Laplace) and the log-Gumbel μ̂ that Table 6.10 already corrects. This is exactly the small, citable clarification a reproduction study exists to generate, and the tone is the point: the thesis reproduced, in full, at the resolution it reports.

Where this sits in the literature

Three findings sit alongside the thesis rather than against it: the two-conventions-in-one-chapter subtlety, the Table 6.9 log-Gumbel μ̂ typo that Table 6.10 itself corrects, and the W_out p-value route that could not be reconstructed as prescribed. The reproduction is essentially exact under the thesis's own stated convention — 35/36 adaptive and 119/120 sealed parameters inside the reporting resolution.

The extension is genuinely new. The thesis's §7.2 names extending the estimators to risk measures as open, and §6.2.2 stops at parameters and p-values — no published work carries these fits through to a 1-in-100 event loss, and none runs a leave-top-k-out stress on this sample. RQ4, RQ5 and RQ6 are therefore not re-derivations, and RQ5 came back refuted.

One inherited verdict is corrected. Klein's own study 02 concluded “skip the diagonal plug-in GLS — it added noise.” Here Σ★ is exact, full, and parameter-free rather than a plug-in, and the GLS weighting is the single largest effect in the method (ARE 0.232 → 0.995 for the Cauchy member; the 2.11× split reproduced at E0005). The correction belongs in the knowledge card at promotion: plug-in diagonal GLS ≠ closed-form full-covariance GLS, and the ARE table says exactly where the difference lives.

The neighbouring robust-severity literature fails differently rather than worse. The trimmed- and Winsorized-moment estimators of the same school trim moments; QLS trims the quantile grid. The family that fits best here has no moments at all, so every moment-based robust estimator is inapplicable to it by construction — while gQLS fits it without complaint, and then C5 shows that fitting it is not the same as being able to price it.

Study lineage. Study 02 was the wind tunnel: on synthetic known-truth severity it measured a 1.083× clean-data robustness cost and, at 10% contamination, a naive-MLE premium error of 352% against 50% for the trimmed estimator. On real data with a real published contamination, this study finds +99.4% vs 0.0% on the 1-in-100 — the same qualitative gap, on a decision unit, against third-party published targets rather than a generator. From study 05 two protocol disciplines carried over and paid: measure the floor that governs your comparison (here one floor's pathology became the RQ5 finding) and report the structure, not the level.

Honest positioning. gQLS is not a frontier architecture and this report makes no claim that it is. What the study contributes is a reproduction carried past the point where the source stops — 156 published parameters rebuilt from scratch, a convention subtlety and a typo localized on the way, and then the fits pushed into a decision unit the source names as future work, where the method's headline claim came apart in a way nobody had measured. The most valuable result is a refutation, and it was registered as a prediction before the loop ran.
